source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: Pooled 22 studies. A one-factor model fits, but loadings are modest. The paper's headline variance figure was later corrected.
numbers: 22 studies, 1,356 groups, 5,279 people, group size 2-7. Standardized loadings 0.27-0.52. Mean inter-task r = 0.27 (0.12-0.50). Leave-one-task-out CI predicted the held-out task at r = 0.40 [0.26, 0.53]. One SD more CI = about 18% higher task performance (plus or minus 12%).
limits: Secondary analysis of one platform (POGS). Task type matters (Sudoku vs unscramble). Only three tasks are common to all studies.
agent_relevance: A weak general factor. Do not assume one scalar predicts all tasks.

source: Correction for Riedl et al. (2022) PNAS 119(19):e2204380119
finding: Correction: average variance extracted (AVE) was wrong because of a software package error. The 44% figure became 19.6%.
numbers: AVE 44% -> 19.6% (loadings 0.27-0.52 unchanged). SI fit changed: Model 1 is saturated (3 indicators, 0 df, fit uninformative). Model 2 (5 tasks) chi2(5)=19.514, CFI=0.93, RMSEA=0.046 [0.026-0.069]. Model 4 (8 tasks) chi2(20, N=1,356)=93.284, CFI=0.833, RMSEA=0.052 [0.042-0.063]; the old text said chi2(28)=466.8.
quote: due to a mistake in a software package, the average variance extracted (AVE) ... are incorrect
limits: The correction says all models still support the one-factor structure. A factor with under 20% shared variance is far weaker than 'over 40%'.
agent_relevance: The c factor explains about one fifth of task variance, not about half. Treat any general group-ability score as weak.

source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses
finding: Meta-analysis of c against outside criterion tasks. c predicts only moderately; member IQ was rarely controlled; independent attempts to reproduce c partly or wholly failed while all Woolley-affiliated ones succeeded.
numbers: c vs criterion r = .26 (95% CI .10, .40), 8 samples, N = 857 groups. Subset that controlled IQ: 5 samples, N = 366 groups; average member IQ vs performance r = .06 (-.08, .20). About 80% of studies underpowered.
quote: We caution against prematurely embracing notions of the c- factor unless it can be independently and robustly replicated
limits: Few studies (K=8). Authors say alternative explanations cannot be dismissed. Written before the 2021 Riedl pool.
agent_relevance: Do not build the agent around a c-style score unless it adds something beyond plain member strength.

source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Table 1: founding studies)
finding: Rowe's table of the early studies. Woolley 2010 Study 1: N=40, first factor 43.4%, c-to-criterion r .52. Study 2: N=152, 44.1%, r .28.
numbers: Engel et al. 2014 face-to-face N=32, 49.3%; online text N=36, 41.4%. Engel 2015 Study 2 N=116, 40%. Credé and Howardson: 6 samples, N=487, factor supported in 5 of 6 by Rowe's coding. Bates and Gupta Studies 2+3 combined N=80.
limits: Small samples in early work. The percentages are first-factor figures, not the corrected CFA AVE.
agent_relevance: Early c numbers came from small groups. Keep a skeptical prior.

source: Credé and Howardson (2017) The structure of group task performance: a second look at collective intelligence (J Appl Psychol 102:1483-1492)
finding: Reanalysis of six samples. The general factor explains little variance in many group tasks. Low-effort responding and nested data may inflate the small covariation. Support for c as a construct is weak.
numbers: 6 samples across 4 studies (per Rowe et al.). Exact first-factor figures not obtained this session.
limits: Seen through a search summary only. Woolley, Kim and Malone (2018) replied that the effort and ability artifacts are not supported by the data.
agent_relevance: A group score may be driven by a few unmotivated or failed runs.

source: Credé and Howardson press coverage (Futurity, Iowa State)
finding: Press summary. Only one of six studies (2014 Indiana University) concluded there was no c. Low motivation, for example a team scoring zero on a 10-minute brick-uses task, can inflate cross-task correlations.
numbers: Six studies; the article gives no sample sizes or variance figures.
limits: Press article, not the paper. Samples were students or community members, not teams working over time.
agent_relevance: Failed runs can create fake correlation across tasks. Filter them before computing any cross-task score.

source: Woolley, Kim and Malone (2018) Measuring collective intelligence in groups: a reply to Credé and Howardson
finding: Reply argues the data do not support the effort and ability explanations. They accept that the evidence is not yet complete.
numbers: No numbers obtained (page returned 403).
limits: Not opened. Described from a search summary only.
agent_relevance: The dispute is not settled by the authors on either side.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence
finding: Independent replication in three studies (312 people). A group factor appeared, but individual IQ explained about 80% of it. Number of women and turn-taking did not predict it.
numbers: 3 studies, 312 people. Study 1 parallel analysis kept one factor: 39.8% of variance, adjusted eigenvalue 1.98 (others 0.85, 0.69, 0.69, 0.79). Study 2 group tasks correlated .31-.66 with each other and .55-.87 with average member Wonderlic. Mean RME predicted group-IQ beta .3 in Study 2 but had no effect on the latent factor in the combined Studies 2-3 SEM.
quote: individual IQ accounted for around 80% of group-IQ differences
limits: Small N (about 80 groups in Studies 2-3). Tasks chosen from Woolley's high-loading ones.
agent_relevance: A group factor can exist and still be mostly member g. For agents, group score may mostly track base-model strength.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: 108 LLM agent groups (8 LLMs; varied size, topology, model mix) tested on 5 tasks. One factor (called ACI) took 66.3% of variance; the second took 18.7%. CFA chi2=30.6, CFI=0.967.
numbers: 108 groups; tasks: commonsense, math, games, coding, writing. Compared with '43%' for human groups. Random forest on group indicators predicted ACI with R2 above 0.8 and single-task performance with R2 above 0.6 on most tasks. Using ACI as a plug-in improved MAS optimisers by 4.6% on unseen tasks.
limits: Compares with the uncorrected human figure; the corrected human AVE is 19.6%. Only 5 tasks, and a stronger base model does well on all of them, so the factor may be a model-strength artifact. No independent replication.
agent_relevance: A big first factor in LLM groups is expected from model strength alone. Do not read it as emergent collective intelligence.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design (indicators)
finding: Skill congruence and average member ability were significant positive predictors of ACI. Group size and effort were not.
numbers: Random-forest importance: skill congruence over 50%, average individual ability 37%; max ability, group size and effort each under 5%. A group with 75% higher API cost had 9.7% lower ACI. Centralised topology cost less than decentralised.
limits: Skill congruence = correlation of agent ability with node degree, defined by the authors. Ability scores come from the same five benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Put the strongest sub-model at the hub of any multi-model loop. More spend or more agents does not add c.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design (generalisation to new tasks)
finding: ACI built from four tasks predicted the fifth task better than the plain average of the four, per the authors.
numbers: Leave-one-task-out over 5 tasks. Mean reciprocal rank above 0.35 for ACI, commonsense and game, so the best group is typically in the top 3. For coding and writing the best group is within the top 6.
limits: Only five tasks, highly correlated across strong models.
agent_relevance: Weak support. ACI mostly says which groups use stronger models.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent coordination in multi-agent language models (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.05174)
finding: Information-theoretic test of whether LLM groups are more than sums of agents. Persona plus 'think about what others might do' prompts moved groups toward complementary roles. The control showed temporal synergy but little coordination.
numbers: GPT-4.1, N=10 agents, T=1, 200 runs per condition (600 total). Success rate was not significantly different across Plain, Persona and Persona+ToM. Replicated with Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Qwen3-235B.
quote: multi-agent LLM systems can be steered with prompt design from mere aggregates to higher-order collectives
limits: One simple guessing game. Group structure changed without success rate changing. By a c-factor author.
agent_relevance: A prompt can create 'collective' structure that does not raise accuracy. Do not count structure as proof of benefit.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent coordination in multi-agent language models (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.05174) (group size and temperature)
finding: Larger groups did worse on the guessing task, as in human groups.
numbers: Grid: group sizes 3-15 x 11 temperatures x 50 runs, GPT-4.1. Each added agent cut success odds by about 8% (OR 0.92, p<1e-16). Each +1 temperature raised odds about 50% (OR 1.50, p<1e-7).
limits: One task and one model in the grid.
agent_relevance: Adding sub-agents has costs. Keep the group small.

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models (Intelligence 106)
finding: Single LLMs already show a positive manifold and a general factor. Authors note human g takes 40-50% of variance and the LLM factor 66%.
numbers: 591 LLMs, 12 benchmarks. General factor 65.6% of variance; mean loading 0.81 (0.64-0.96). Model fit chi2(44)=250.42, CFI .984, RMSEA .089. Parameter count correlated with the factor, with diminishing returns.
limits: Leaderboard data across models. May reflect training and scale rather than one ability. Authors leave open achievement vs intelligence.
agent_relevance: A big general factor is normal across LLMs, so ACI's 66.3% is not special evidence for c.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Debate systems do not reliably beat self-consistency or single-agent prompting. Tuning matters a lot.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo. MedQA (1,273 Qs) best: Medprompt .65, Society of Mind .64, Ensemble Refinement .64, Self-Consistency .60, single agent .60, Multi-Persona .58. GPQA (448): single agent .33 vs SoM .27. PubMedQA (500): single .75, SoM .74.
limits: Small model. Best-of-runs vs median differ a lot. Hyperparameters tuned per dataset.
agent_relevance: A group of copies is not smarter by default. A tuned single-agent ensemble is a hard baseline.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs (agreement intensity)
finding: Telling agents how often to agree (0-100%) changed results by dataset. High agreement helped MedQA and PubMedQA but hurt CIAR.
numbers: Multi-Persona about +15% on USMLE, Society of Mind about +5%, ChatEval barely moved. Multi-Persona went from worst to best protocol on MedQA.
limits: Dataset-specific tuning risks overfit to the benchmark.
agent_relevance: No fixed consensus level is best. Settings need per-task tuning.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Five debate methods on nine benchmarks and four models often fail to beat chain-of-thought and self-consistency despite more compute.
numbers: With GPT-4o-mini, Society of Mind scored below CoT on all nine datasets in Table 3. Adding rounds or agents did not help consistently.
limits: Position paper. Table text partly garbled by PDF extraction.
agent_relevance: Same-model debate is a weak lever.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate (model heterogeneity)
finding: Randomly mixing GPT-4o-mini and Llama3.1-70b (p=0.5 each) inside debate raised results.
numbers: SoM-Heter average 76.7 vs CoT-average 72.5 (+5.8%); SoM-Llama alone 69.9; SoM-GPT 74.3.
limits: Two model families only.
agent_relevance: Diversity of model, not number of agents, is the lever.

source: Li, Naito and Shirado (2025) HiddenBench: assessing collective reasoning in multi-agent LLMs via hidden profile tasks
finding: LLM groups fail to pool unshared information, like human groups. Prompts did not fix it. Scale and reasoning did not either.
numbers: GPT-4.1: Hidden Profile post-discussion accuracy 0.233 vs Full Profile 0.733 (p<.001), 30 sessions each. Humans 0.385 vs 0.604 (p=.003), 8 sessions each. 15 LLMs, 65 tasks. Gemini-2.5-Pro best at 0.671; Flash 0.550; Flash-Lite 0.394.
limits: Few sessions in Study 1. One paradigm.
agent_relevance: Direct test of group information integration. Make critical facts shared across sub-agents, not held by one.

source: Li, Naito and Shirado (2025) HiddenBench (prompting)
finding: Five prompts from extremely cooperative to extremely conflictual, plus zero-shot CoT and telling agents about the information asymmetry, gave almost no gain. GPT-5 variants did not clearly beat GPT-4.1-Mini in groups.
numbers: Only the extremely conflictual prompt gave modest gains under the average rule. Human groups averaged 53.4 messages, longer than LLM groups.
limits: One model (GPT-4.1) in the prompt study.
agent_relevance: Prompt fixes for group reasoning are weak; premature consensus is the failure.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups (predictors)
finding: Collaboration process (skill congruence, strategy, effort) was the biggest predictor, then member skill, then composition.
numbers: Effort not significant on its own. Proportion of women predicted CI only without controlling social perceptiveness. Age diversity negative. Coefficients are in SI Table S5, not seen.
limits: Process variables came from the same sessions as the outcome.
agent_relevance: Skill-aware routing (who does what) is the main robust lever.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups (critiques noted)
finding: The paper itself says some studies question the CI factor and results vary by task. It cites Credé and Howardson 2017 and Barlow and Dennis 2016 as critiques.
numbers: Eight task types; three in every study (Brainstorm Object, Typing Text, Unscramble Words).
limits: It does not describe the critiques in detail.
agent_relevance: Different tasks load differently; do not collapse them into one score.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups (Wikipedia note)
finding: The opened text has no Wikipedia mention and no 'Wikipedia task V'. The brief's 'V via Wikipedia' was not found.
numbers: None.
limits: Main text only; SI not read.
agent_relevance: Cite the PNAS correction notice for the 44% to 19.6% change.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330:686-688)
finding: Founding claim: one factor explains over 40% of group task variance, weakly tied to mean or max member IQ, tied to social sensitivity, turn-taking equality and share of women.
numbers: Figures via Rowe et al. table: 43.4% and 44.1% (see c04). Mean member IQ vs c r about .19 and .15.
limits: Not opened directly. Numbers come from secondary sources.
agent_relevance: This is the claim under dispute.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris and Malone (2014) Reading the mind in the eyes or reading between the lines
finding: Online text-chat groups also showed a factor, so face-to-face is not required.
numbers: Per Rowe table: face-to-face N=32 groups, 49.3%; online text N=36 groups, 41.4%.
limits: Same lab as the original. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Replication by the original authors only.

source: Burton et al. (2024) How large language models can reshape collective intelligence (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Perspective: LLMs are both tools for and products of collective intelligence. Risks include homogenised opinion.
numbers: None obtained.
limits: Seen as a search listing only.
agent_relevance: Many agents of one model can reduce diversity.
